steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on the behavior and convergence of local Bayesian optimization. Motivate it with BO's trouble in high dimensions and the empirical success of local methods, note the missing theory, and lay out the questions we study and our contributions.

- Local BO: empirical promise, missing theory
- Our study: two questions (Q1 solution quality, Q2 convergence)
- Findings for Q1 and Q2
- Contributions

  - global BO well studied under controlled assumptions; little known about local BO behavior/convergence in same settings; literature mostly empirical, real-world applications

  - Q1: under common assumptions (e.g. objective is GP sample path, known hyperparameters), how good are local solutions?

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Bayesian optimization (BO) is one of the most well studied and successful algorithms for solving black-box optimization problems. It has wide ranging applications, from hyperparameter tuning and reinforcement learning, to recent applications in small molecule and sequence design. Despite this success, the curse of dimensionality has been a challenge for the framework for a long time. The cumulative regret of BO scales exponentially with the dimensionality of the search space, unless strong assumptions like additive structure hold. In practice, BO has historically struggled on optimization problems with more than a handful of dimensions.

Recently, local approaches to Bayesian optimization have shown great promise empirically for high-dimensional optimization problems. The approach makes intuitive sense: a typical claim is that a local optimum can be found relatively quickly, and that exponential sample complexity is only needed if you want to enumerate all local optima. But these intuitions have not been fully formalized. Global Bayesian optimization is well studied under controlled assumptions, but little is known about how local Bayesian optimization behaves or converges in these same settings, and the related literature mostly focuses on strong empirical results on real-world applications.

- Our study
  - behavior + convergence rates of local BO under the same assumptions used for global BO
  - Q1: under common assumptions (e.g. objective is GP sample path, known hyperparameters), how good are local solutions?

  - Q2: first theoretical convergence analysis of a local BO algorithm: GIBO (prior work), slightly modified
  - open questions: impact of noise; harder optimization near a stationary point

  3. looseness of bound: empirical uncertainty reduction of GIBO policy vs upper bound

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Bayesian optimization (BO) is one of the most well studied and successful algorithms for solving black-box optimization problems. It has wide ranging applications, from hyperparameter tuning and reinforcement learning, to recent applications in small molecule and sequence design. Despite this success, the curse of dimensionality has been a challenge for the framework for a long time. The cumulative regret of BO scales exponentially with the dimensionality of the search space, unless strong assumptions like additive structure hold. In practice, BO has historically struggled on optimization problems with more than a handful of dimensions.

Recently, local approaches to Bayesian optimization have shown great promise empirically for high-dimensional optimization problems. The approach makes intuitive sense: a typical claim is that a local optimum can be found relatively quickly, and that exponential sample complexity is only needed if you want to enumerate all local optima. But these intuitions have not been fully formalized. Global Bayesian optimization is well studied under controlled assumptions, but little is known about how local Bayesian optimization behaves or converges in these same settings, and the related literature mostly focuses on strong empirical results on real-world applications.

In this paper, we start to close this gap. We investigate the behavior of local BO and prove convergence rates for it, under the same well-studied assumptions that are commonly used to analyze global BO. We split our study of the properties of local BO into two questions:

- Q1 Under common assumptions (for example, when the objective function is a sample path from a GP with known hyperparameters), how good are the local solutions that local BO converges to?

- Q2 Under the same assumptions, is there a local Bayesian optimization procedure that is guaranteed to find a local solution, and how fast can it do so?

For Q1, we find empirically that local BO behaves in a surprising way on “typical” high dimensional Gaussian process sample paths: even a single run of local BO, without random restarts, gives shockingly good objective values in high dimension. We can characterize “surprise” here by the minimum equivalent grid search size that is needed to achieve this value in expectation. See Figure 1 and more discussions in § 3.

For Q2, we give the first theoretical convergence analysis of a local BO algorithm, GIBO as presented in prior work, with slight modifications. Our results bring up a number of natural questions about local Bayesian optimization, such as the impact of noise and how optimization gets more and more challenging as local BO approaches a stationary point.

Our contributions are the following:

- 1. We give upper bounds on the uncertainty of the gradient when it is actively learned with the GIBO procedure from prior work, in both the noiseless and the noisy settings.

- 2. We relate these uncertainty bounds to the bias in the gradient estimate that is used at each step, and this lets us translate the results into convergence rates for both noiseless and noisy functions.

- 3. We investigate how loose our bound is by studying the empirical reduction in uncertainty that is achieved with the GIBO policy and comparing it to our upper bound.

- 4. We empirically study the quality of individual local solutions found by a local Bayesian optimization, a slightly modified version of GIBO, on GP sample paths.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Bayesian optimization (BO) [1] is among the most well studied and successful algorithms for solving black-box optimization problems, with wide ranging applications from hyperparameter tuning [2] and reinforcement learning [3,4] to recent applications in small molecule [5,6,7,8,9] and sequence design [10]. Despite its success, the curse of dimensionality has long been a challenge for the framework. Cumulative regret for BO scales exponentially with the dimensionality of the search space unless strong assumptions like additive structure [11] are met. Empirically, BO has historically struggled on problems with more than a handful of dimensions.

Recently, local approaches to Bayesian optimization have empirically shown great promise in addressing high-dimensional optimization problems [12,3,13,4,14]. The approach is intuitively appealing: a typical claim is that a local optimum can be found relatively quickly, and exponential sample complexity is only necessary if one wishes to enumerate all local optima. However, these intuitions have not been fully formalized. While global Bayesian optimization is well studied under controlled assumptions [15,16], little is known about the behavior or convergence properties of local Bayesian optimization in these same settings; the related literature focuses mostly on strong empirical results on real-world applications.

In this paper, we begin to close this gap by investigating the behavior of local BO and proving convergence rates for it under the same well-studied assumptions commonly used to analyze global BO. We divide our study of the properties of local BO into two questions:

- Q1 Using common assumptions (e.g., when the objective function is a sample path from a GP with known hyperparameters), how good are the local solutions that local BO converges to?

- Q2 Under these same assumptions, is there a local Bayesian optimization procedure that is guaranteed to find a local solution, and how quickly can it do so?

For Q1, we find empirically that the behavior of local BO on “typical” high dimensional Gaussian process sample paths is surprising: even a single run of local BO, without random restarts, yields shockingly good objective values in high dimension. Here, we characterize “surprise” by the minimum equivalent grid search size necessary to achieve this value in expectation. See Figure 1 and more discussions in § 3.

For Q2, we present the first theoretical convergence analysis of a local BO algorithm, GIBO as presented in [3] with slight modifications. Our results bring into focus a number of natural questions about local Bayesian optimization, such as the impact of noise and the increasing challenges of optimization as local BO approaches a stationary point.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

- 1. We provide upper bounds on the uncertainty of the gradient when actively learned using the GIBO procedure described in [3], in both the noiseless and noisy settings.

- 2. By relating these uncertainty bounds to the bias in the gradient estimate used at each step, we translate these results into convergence rates for both noiseless and noisy functions.

- 3. We investigate the looseness of our bound by studying the empirical reduction in uncertainty achieved by the GIBO policy and comparing it to our upper bound.

- 4. We empirically study the quality of individual local solutions found by a local Bayesian optimization, a slightly modified version of GIBO, on GP sample paths.
